newsitem.title: USA: Car prices key in Oct core PPI - US Labor economist.
newsitem.headline: Car prices key in Oct core PPI - US Labor economist.

text.p: Plummeting passenger car prices were a main factor in the decline in the core Producer Price Index (PPI) for October, an economist with the U.S. Labor Department said Wednesday.

Brett Graff, economist with the Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics, noted that passenger cars make up 11.1 percent of the closely watched core PPI, which excludes the volatile food and energy prices.
She also pointed out that seasonal factors were at play in the decline in passenger car prices.
The department reported earlier that overall the PPI climbed 0.4 percent, posting its biggest rise since March of this year.
However, the core PPI fell 0.3 percent, the sharpest drop in two years.
On a seasonally adjusted basis, passenger car prices fell 1.6 percent, although before seasonal adjustment, those prices were up 5.2 percent.
Big decreases in prices of light motor trucks and heavy motor trucks also were also a prominent factor in the core PPI decline, Graff said.

Light motor truck prices fell 1.2 percent, while heavy motor trucks fell 4.4 percent. New model introductions for light motor trucks tend to follow a similar pattern to passenger cars, although the pattern for heavy trucks is different, Graff said.
Light and heavy trucks are part of the capital equipment index in the PPI, which accounts for 40 percent of core PPI.
Another component of the capital equipment index, computers, posted a 2.0 percent drop in October.
Turning to the overall PPI, which rose due to both higher food and energy prices, Graff said the surge in energy prices was tied to lower inventories for crude oil.
The stocks had been depleted during last year's unusually cold winter, causing a price rise once demand for heating oil began to rise again this fall, she said.
Increases in pork, fresh and dry vegetables, and fish and shellfish pushed food prices up in October.
Graff said the rise in pork prices was tied to higher feeding costs as well as to high export demand.
